# Returns true if the string looks like an email address.
#
# This is a plausibility check, not full RFC 5322 validation: it requires
# one "@", a non-empty local part, and a dotted domain, with no whitespace.
# The only way to know an address really works is to send mail to it.
EMAIL_PATTERN = /\A[^@\s]+@[^@\s.]+(\.[^@\s.]+)+\z/

def email?(string)
  string.is_a?(String) && string.match?(EMAIL_PATTERN)
end

`email.rb` defines `email?(string)`, which returns true when the string has exactly one `@`, a non-empty local part, a domain with at least one dot, and no whitespace. I ran it against a handful of valid and invalid cases and all came out as expected.

```ruby
EMAIL_PATTERN = /\A[^@\s]+@[^@\s.]+(\.[^@\s.]+)+\z/

def email?(string)
  string.is_a?(String) && string.match?(EMAIL_PATTERN)
end
```

It is deliberately a plausibility check rather than full RFC validation, so it rejects dotless domains like `user@localhost`. Non-strings such as `nil` return false rather than raising.

Ruby's standard library also ships `URI::MailTo::EMAIL_REGEXP` if you'd rather use a stricter built-in pattern; note that one accepts dotless domains.
